sentences.text: Nigersaurus was a small sauropod measuring between 9 and 14.1 meters in length with a short neck.
This animal had a body length of 9 to 14.1 meters and a femur of only 1 meter, weighing 1.9 to 4 metric tons.
Some skull fossils were so thin that light beams could pass through them.
The connecting bone struts in the skull were usually less than 2 millimeters thick.
Nigersaurus had presacral vertebrae that were so hollow they formed a column of thin shells separated by septa.
Nigersaurus holds the record for the highest tooth replacement rate of any known dinosaur.
It replaced its teeth faster than any other known dinosaur, with a replacement rate of once every fourteen days.
Nigersaurus likely had one of the weakest bites among sauropods due to weak jaw muscles.
The genus Nigersaurus was formally described by Sereno and colleagues in 1999.
Initial remains were discovered during a 1965–1972 expedition led by Philippe Taquet and first published in 1976.
Nigersaurus was discovered in the Elrhaz Formation at a site called Gadoufaoua in the Republic of Niger.
Researchers believe Nigersaurus was a browser that fed on vegetation close to the ground.
It inhabited a riparian environment and likely ate soft plants including ferns, horsetails, and angiosperms.
Grooves at the front of the jaws indicate the presence of a keratinous sheath.
Despite having large nostrils, Nigersaurus had an underdeveloped olfactory brain region and likely lacked an advanced sense of smell.
Nigersaurus had eyes positioned high on its skull above the muzzle, providing overlapping fields of view.
Nigersaurus could gather and crop food within 1 meter of the ground surface.
In 2017, Lucio M. Ibiricu and colleagues suggested that postcranial pneumatization in rebbachisaurids was an adaptation to decrease skeletal density.
Nigersaurus belongs to the subfamily Rebbachisaurinae of the family Rebbachisauridae within the sauropod superfamily Diplodocoidea.
Nigersaurus was originally classified as a dicraeosaurid in 1976 but was reclassified as a rebbachisaurid diplodocoid in 1999.
Nigersaurus lived during the Aptian to Albian stages of the Cretaceous period.
Nigersaurus lived during the mid-Cretaceous period, approximately 115 to 105 million years ago, between the Aptian and Albian ages.
Nigersaurus lived from the Aptian to the Albian stages, between 121.4 and 100.5 million years ago.
There is an ongoing debate regarding whether Nigersaurus held its head habitually downwards or horizontally.
A 2009 study contested whether the downturned head posture was the habitual one for Nigersaurus.
It is debated whether Nigersaurus habitually held its head down or horizontally like other sauropods, with the horizontal position being favored.
